bib.title: Statistical Rethinking, Chapter 8: Markov Chain Monte Carlo
bib.venue: book chapter (Statistical Rethinking, pp. 241-265; edition not printed in the chapter)

question: How can posterior distributions be sampled with MCMC (Metropolis, Gibbs, HMC via Stan) and how do you check that a chain is healthy?
contributions: Introduces Metropolis, Gibbs sampling and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
Introduces map2stan (rethinking package) to fit map formula lists with Stan HMC
Gives diagnostics (trace plot, n_eff, Rhat) and two pathological examples (flat priors, non-identifiable parameters) fixed with weakly informative priors

limits: HMC needs continuous parameters; discrete parameters (e.g. imputing discrete missing data) cannot be handled by HMC alone.
HMC must be tuned (mass and other algorithm parameters); Stan automates much of this.
Rhat can reach 1.00 even for an invalid chain: a signal of danger, never of safety.
Gibbs sampling needs conjugate pairs and becomes very inefficient with hundreds to tens of thousands of parameters.
The chapter uses the old rethinking/map2stan interface, rstan and R, with HPDI and DIC/WAIC; it predates PyMC-style workflows and newer diagnostics (bulk/tail ESS, divergences, rank-normalised Rhat).
Informal introduction: no formal proof of convergence, no divergence-transition discussion, and non-identifiability is shown only on toy examples.
practices: Preprocess all variable transformations before fitting and pass Stan a trimmed data frame with only the used variables, since NA in unused variables makes Stan refuse (8.3.1).
Read n_eff and Rhat: Rhat should approach 1.00 from above; even 1.01 is suspicious and 1.10 a catastrophe (8.4.3).
Check trace plots first for stationarity and good mixing (8.3.6).
Treat warmup as adaptation, not burn-in; extract.samples drops it (8.3.6, 8.4.1).
Use four short chains to check, one long chain for inference (8.4.2).
When debugging use a single chain; use 3 or 4 chains to confirm chains converge to the same region (8.4.2).
Do not use flat priors; add weakly informative priors (e.g. Normal, half-Cauchy for sd) to tame wandering chains and speed sampling (8.4.3, 8.4.4).
Slow sampling often signals an under-identified or bad model (Gelman's folk theorem of statistical computing) (8.4.4).
Sporadic Stan 'Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected' messages, especially in warmup, are usually harmless (8.3 Overthinking).
Do not rely on a single diagnostic; Rhat and n_eff are heuristics (8.4.2 Rethinking).

terms.definition: Propose a symmetric move; move with probability equal to the ratio of the proposal's to the current posterior density (probability of moving = shells/stones in the fable).
A more general method that allows asymmetric proposals.
A variant of Metropolis-Hastings that uses adaptive proposals computed from conjugate pairs of prior and likelihood.
Runs a physics simulation of a frictionless particle gliding over the log-posterior surface; the gradient determines when it turns around.
Samples used to adapt the sampler; not part of the target posterior and not the same as burn-in.
A crude estimate of the number of independent samples obtained.
The Gelman-Rubin convergence diagnostic; should approach 1.00 from above.
The path staying within the posterior distribution, with a stable mean from beginning to end.
Each successive sample is not highly correlated with the one before it; rapid zig-zag in the trace.
Distribution of the ratio of two Gaussian draws; location x0 and scale gamma; no defined mean or variance.
Parameters, such as a1 and a2 in mu = a1 + a2, of which only the sum can be estimated.

figures.caption: Trace plot of the Markov chain from the ruggedness model, m8.1stan: clean, stationary, well-mixing; gray region is warmup.
figures.why: Reference picture of a healthy chain.

figures.caption: Diagnosing and healing a sick Markov chain. Top: two chains from m8.2 not stationary. Bottom: weakly informative priors (m8.3) fix it.
figures.why: Side-by-side of a sick chain and a healthy chain.

figures.caption: Prior (dashed) and posterior (blue) for the model with weakly informative priors, m8.3.
figures.why: Shows weak priors are washed out by two observations yet make estimation possible.

figures.caption: Left: chain with wandering parameters a1, a2 from m8.4. Right: same model with weakly informative priors, m8.5.
figures.why: Shows what non-identifiability looks like in a trace plot.

code.snippet:
proposal <- current + sample( c(-1,1) , size=1 )
if ( proposal < 1 ) proposal <- 10
if ( proposal > 10 ) proposal <- 1
prob_move <- proposal/current
current <- ifelse( runif(1) < prob_move , proposal , current )

m8.1stan <- map2stan(
alist(
log_gdp ~ dnorm( mu , sigma ) ,
mu <- a + bR*rugged + bA*cont_africa + bAR*rugged*cont_africa ,
a ~ dnorm(0,100),
bR ~ dnorm(0,10),
bA ~ dnorm(0,10),
bAR ~ dnorm(0,10),
sigma ~ dcauchy(0,2)
) ,
data=dd.trim )
